title: "Training models"
subtitle: "Fit a text model only after the example set is large enough"
description: "Learn why a 28-sentence pilot cannot evaluate a model and fit penalized logistic regression on inaugural paragraphs."
categories: [model development, training models, text classification]
---

Maya's folder of sentence labels helped the team agree on its annotation
categories. Those categories cover training, scheduling, skills, requirements,
and other workforce details.

The team now needs a predictor. Data that help people learn a codebook can
still be too limited for model evaluation.

This lesson uses the Riverton set only for a pilot check. Model development
uses the larger public corpus of presidential inaugural paragraphs bundled
with quanteda.

::: {.callout-note}
The Riverton Workforce Lab, its job board, and its training flyer are fictional
teaching materials. The inaugural addresses are works of the United States
government. This lesson treats them as public domain text packaged by quanteda.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

This lesson shows how to:

- explain when a labeled set is too small for a test of a model.
- use a larger teaching corpus after the labeling pilot.
- distinguish a recipe, model specification, workflow, fit, and prediction.
- compare candidate models without using the final test set.
- fit the selected penalized logistic regression model.
- report a live score with a baseline and limits attached.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Stop at the pilot set

A **training set** is the labeled material a model learns from. A **test set** is
labeled material reserved for scoring. In a small test set, one correct or
incorrect prediction can greatly affect the score.

```{r}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(readr)
  library(dplyr)
  library(tibble)
  library(rsample)
  library(recipes)
  library(textrecipes)
  library(parsnip)
  library(workflows)
  library(yardstick)
  library(glmnet)
})

riverton_sentences <- read_csv(
  "data/workforce/workforce_sentences.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    sentence_id = col_character(),
    document_id = col_character(),
    source_line = col_character(),
    text = col_character(),
    reference_label = col_character(),
    uncertainty = col_character(),
    annotator_id = col_character(),
    rationale = col_character(),
    codebook_version = col_character(),
    codebook_hash = col_character(),
    derived = col_character(),
    transformation = col_character()
  )
)

set.seed(4300)
riverton_split <- group_initial_split(
  riverton_sentences,
  group = document_id,
  prop = 0.75
)
riverton_training <- training(riverton_split)
riverton_testing <- testing(riverton_split)

riverton_label_counts <- riverton_sentences |>
  count(reference_label, name = "sentences") |>
  arrange(desc(sentences), reference_label)

split_size <- tibble(
  part = c("training", "test"),
  rows = c(nrow(riverton_training), nrow(riverton_testing))
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  riverton_label_counts,
  col.names = c("Label", "Sentences"),
  caption = "The Riverton pilot labels are too few for a model score",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  split_size,
  col.names = c("Split part", "Rows"),
  caption = "Keeping documents whole leaves only four test sentences",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(riverton_sentences), 28L),
  identical(n_distinct(riverton_sentences$reference_label), 5L),
  identical(nrow(riverton_training), 24L),
  identical(nrow(riverton_testing), 4L),
  identical(n_distinct(riverton_training$document_id), 6L),
  identical(n_distinct(riverton_testing$document_id), 1L),
  identical(
    intersect(
      riverton_training$document_id,
      riverton_testing$document_id
    ),
    character()
  ),
  identical(sum(riverton_label_counts$sentences), 28L)
)
```

The split is deterministic because the seed is `4300`, and it keeps all rows
from a source document together. It leaves `r nrow(riverton_testing)` test
sentences from one document, containing
`r n_distinct(riverton_testing$reference_label)` of the five labels.
A single changed answer would move accuracy by about
`r round(100 / nrow(riverton_testing), 1)` percentage points. A test set this
small cannot give a reliable estimate of prediction performance.

## Use a larger corpus

The shared helper reads the larger corpus from
`quanteda::data_corpus_inaugural`. Each row contains one paragraph of at
least 25 words. The **era** outcome distinguishes addresses before 1900 from
addresses in 1900 or later.

```{r}
source("R/inaugural-corpus.R")

paragraphs <- inaugural_paragraphs()

corpus_summary <- tibble(
  measure = c("paragraphs", "speeches", "people", "surnames"),
  value = c(
    nrow(paragraphs),
    n_distinct(paragraphs$speech_id),
    n_distinct(paragraphs$president),
    n_distinct(paragraphs$surname)
  )
)

era_counts <- paragraphs |>
  group_by(era) |>
  summarise(
    paragraphs = n(),
    median_words = median(paragraph_words),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  corpus_summary,
  col.names = c("Measure", "Value"),
  caption = "The inaugural paragraph corpus used for model training",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  era_counts,
  col.names = c("Era", "Paragraphs", "Median paragraph words"),
  caption = "Paragraphs by era",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(paragraphs), 1377L),
  identical(n_distinct(paragraphs$speech_id), 60L),
  identical(n_distinct(paragraphs$president), 40L),
  identical(n_distinct(paragraphs$surname), 36L),
  "paragraph_words" %in% names(paragraphs),
  identical(as.integer(era_counts$paragraphs), c(485L, 892L)),
  identical(as.numeric(era_counts$median_words), c(112, 54)),
  identical(levels(paragraphs$era), c("before 1900", "1900 or later"))
)
```

The material has `r format(nrow(paragraphs), big.mark = ",")` paragraphs from
`r n_distinct(paragraphs$speech_id)` speeches by `r n_distinct(paragraphs$president)` people.
The helper retains both the full name in `president` and the `surname`.
Grouping by surname alone would merge different people with the same family
name.

Paragraphs before 1900 have median length
`r era_counts$median_words[era_counts$era == "before 1900"]`. Later
paragraphs have median length
`r era_counts$median_words[era_counts$era == "1900 or later"]`.

This corpus does not represent all political speech or all historical writing.
It gives the lesson enough held-out paragraphs to examine a specific claim
about these speeches.

## Keep the final test set out of model selection

The split keeps each speech whole. Paragraphs from one inaugural address cannot
appear in both training and test sets.
The seed is `4301` for the split.

The test speeches provide an estimate of performance after model selection. Selection based
on test scores would reuse final evaluation evidence. This internal holdout
comes from a corpus used throughout the section. It does not confirm
performance on new text from another source.

Inside the training set, **cross-validation** makes several temporary
train-and-check splits. Each temporary check is called a **fold**. The folds are
often called **CV folds**. They are grouped by speech here, so every paragraph
from one address stays together. Five folds put 9 or 10 speeches in each
held-out set while leaving both era labels represented.

```{r}
baselines <- read_csv(
  "data/inaugural/baselines.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    task = col_character(),
    outcome = col_character(),
    rows = col_integer(),
    speeches = col_integer(),
    people = col_integer(),
    largest_class = col_character(),
    baseline_accuracy = col_double()
  )
)

model_comparison <- read_csv(
  "data/inaugural/model-comparison.csv",
  na = "",
  col_types = cols(
    rank = col_integer(),
    candidate = col_character(),
    family = col_character(),
    penalty = col_double(),
    mtry = col_integer(),
    min_n = col_integer(),
    mean_bal_accuracy = col_double(),
    std_err_bal_accuracy = col_double(),
    mean_accuracy = col_double(),
    std_err_accuracy = col_double(),
    selected = col_logical(),
    selection_reason = col_character()
  )
)

fold_summary <- read_csv(
  "data/inaugural/model-comparison-folds.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    fold = col_character(),
    analysis_speeches = col_integer(),
    assessment_speeches = col_integer(),
    assessment_paragraphs = col_integer(),
    before_1900 = col_integer(),
    later_1900 = col_integer()
  )
)

set.seed(4301)
era_split <- group_initial_split(
  paragraphs,
  group = speech_id,
  prop = 0.75
)
era_training <- training(era_split)
era_testing <- testing(era_split)

set.seed(4310)
era_folds <- group_vfold_cv(
  era_training,
  group = speech_id,
  v = 5,
  strata = era,
  balance = "groups"
)

fold_group_overlap <- vapply(
  era_folds$splits,
  \(split) {
    length(intersect(
      unique(analysis(split)$speech_id),
      unique(assessment(split)$speech_id)
    ))
  },
  integer(1)
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  fold_summary,
  col.names = c(
    "Fold",
    "Training speeches",
    "Held-out speeches",
    "Held-out paragraphs",
    "Before 1900",
    "1900 or later"
  ),
  caption = "Five grouped folds inside the training speeches",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(era_training), 1042L),
  identical(nrow(era_testing), 335L),
  identical(n_distinct(era_training$speech_id), 46L),
  identical(n_distinct(era_testing$speech_id), 14L),
  identical(nrow(era_folds), 5L),
  all(fold_group_overlap == 0L),
  identical(fold_summary$assessment_speeches, c(10L, 9L, 9L, 9L, 9L)),
  all(fold_summary$before_1900 > 0L),
  all(fold_summary$later_1900 > 0L)
)
```

Stratification distributes early and later speeches across the folds. It does
not equalize paragraph counts. The table shows that the paragraph-level class
mix still varies, which is one reason balanced accuracy is the primary measure.

## Compare a small set of candidates

This is not a search across every model R can fit. The comparison asks whether a
different kind of decision rule changes the answer:

- **Ridge logistic regression** retains every word feature but reduces the
  magnitudes of fitted weights toward zero.
- **Lasso logistic regression** uses the same linear model but can set some word
  weights exactly to zero.
- A **random forest** combines many branching rules and can learn relationships
  that are not linear.

**Tuning parameters** control how each candidate learns. The comparison uses
four ridge penalties from `0.01` to `10` and four lasso penalties from
`0.0001` to `0.1`. Their fitted penalty paths use different scales. One
shared grid would include duplicate or intercept-only fits without adding
useful comparisons.

The forest uses six combinations of features per split (`mtry`) and minimum
rows per branch (`min_n`). The builder in `data-raw/build-model-comparison.R`
fits all 14 settings: four ridge, four lasso, and six forest. It never reads
the final test speeches.

Balanced accuracy is the primary selection measure because it gives the two era
classes equal weight. Raw accuracy appears beside it so the effect of the
uneven class counts stays visible.

The table shows the two leading ridge settings and the leading lasso and forest
settings. The ridge means differ, but their fold-to-fold standard errors overlap.
Five related folds do not provide a confidence interval for other corpora.

```{r}
comparison_display <- model_comparison |>
  filter(selected | rank %in% c(2L, 3L, 5L)) |>
  mutate(
    setting = case_when(
      candidate == "random forest" ~
        paste0("mtry ", mtry, "; min_n ", min_n),
      TRUE ~ paste0("penalty ", penalty)
    ),
    chosen = if_else(selected, "yes", "no")
  ) |>
  select(
    candidate,
    setting,
    mean_bal_accuracy,
    std_err_bal_accuracy,
    mean_accuracy,
    chosen
  )

selected_candidate <- model_comparison |>
  filter(selected)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  comparison_display |>
    mutate(
      across(
        c(
          mean_bal_accuracy,
          std_err_bal_accuracy,
          mean_accuracy
        ),
        \(value) round(value, 4)
      )
    ),
  col.names = c(
    "Candidate",
    "Setting",
    "Mean balanced accuracy",
    "Standard error",
    "Mean accuracy",
    "Chosen"
  ),
  caption = "Leading settings from 14 candidates compared on training folds",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(model_comparison), 14L),
  identical(nrow(comparison_display), 4L),
  identical(sum(model_comparison$selected), 1L),
  identical(selected_candidate$candidate, "ridge logistic"),
  identical(selected_candidate$penalty, 0.01),
  identical(round(selected_candidate$mean_bal_accuracy, 4), 0.8008),
  identical(
    round(
      model_comparison$mean_bal_accuracy[
        model_comparison$candidate == "ridge logistic" &
          model_comparison$penalty == 0.1
      ],
      4
    ),
    0.7901
  ),
  identical(
    round(
      model_comparison$mean_bal_accuracy[
        model_comparison$candidate == "lasso logistic" &
          model_comparison$penalty == 0.001
      ],
      4
    ),
    0.7809
  )
)
```

Ridge with penalty `0.01` has the highest mean balanced accuracy,
`r round(selected_candidate$mean_bal_accuracy, 4)`. The fold-to-fold standard
errors overlap those of the nearby candidates, so the table does not
establish the best model for every corpus. The lesson retains ridge because it
ranks first here and provides a linear model. Lesson 45 examines its
coefficients.

The selected penalty is the lowest ridge value tried. Less **shrinkage**, or
reduction in coefficient magnitudes, helped among these four settings. That
does not establish `0.01` as the best possible penalty. A complete search
would extend the grid before making that claim.

The random forest is a useful check rather than a required upgrade. Its best raw
accuracy is competitive, but its lower balanced accuracy shows that more correct
paragraphs can still mean less even performance across classes.

## Build the selected workflow

A tidymodels pipeline has four parts:

1. A **recipe** is a set of instructions that converts raw text into numeric model
   columns. Each `step_*()` line adds one instruction.
2. A **model specification** names the model family and its settings before
   fitting.
3. An **engine** names the package that performs the calculations. Here that
   package is glmnet.
4. A **workflow** keeps the recipe and model specification together. **Fitting**
   uses training data to estimate model weights.

The recipe converts text into model columns. **Tf-idf** means term frequency times
inverse document frequency. A word gets more weight in a paragraph when it is
common there and rare elsewhere. The recipe first removes stop words such as
`the` and `of`. It then retains the 500 most frequent
remaining tokens.

The selected model is **logistic regression**, a linear classifier for
categories. The penalty reduces coefficient magnitudes toward zero to limit
the model's response to incidental patterns in the training text.

```{r}
text_recipe <- recipe(era ~ paragraph, data = era_training) |>
  step_tokenize(paragraph) |>
  step_stopwords(paragraph) |>
  step_tokenfilter(paragraph, max_tokens = 500) |>
  step_tfidf(paragraph)

text_model <- logistic_reg(penalty = 0.01, mixture = 0) |>
  set_engine("glmnet")

era_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(text_recipe) |>
  add_model(text_model)

set.seed(4302)
era_fitted <- fit(era_workflow, data = era_training)

era_predictions <- predict(era_fitted, era_testing) |>
  bind_cols(era_testing |> select(era))

live_metrics <- metric_set(accuracy, bal_accuracy)(
  era_predictions,
  truth = era,
  estimate = .pred_class
)
live_accuracy <- live_metrics |>
  filter(.metric == "accuracy") |>
  pull(.estimate)
live_bal_accuracy <- live_metrics |>
  filter(.metric == "bal_accuracy") |>
  pull(.estimate)

corpus_baseline <- baselines |>
  filter(task == "era") |>
  pull(baseline_accuracy)

training_majority <- era_training |>
  count(era, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice(1) |>
  pull(era)

split_baseline_accuracy <- mean(era_testing$era == training_majority)

score_table <- tibble(
  measure = c(
    "Final test accuracy",
    "Final test balanced accuracy",
    "Same-split training-majority rule",
    "Corpus largest-class baseline"
  ),
  value = c(
    live_accuracy,
    live_bal_accuracy,
    split_baseline_accuracy,
    corpus_baseline
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  score_table |>
    mutate(value = round(value, 4)),
  col.names = c("Measure", "Value"),
  caption = "One held-out test after candidate selection",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(round(live_accuracy, 4), 0.8209),
  identical(round(live_bal_accuracy, 4), 0.8361),
  identical(round(split_baseline_accuracy, 4), 0.4179),
  identical(round(corpus_baseline, 4), 0.6478),
  all(era_predictions$.pred_class %in% levels(paragraphs$era))
)
```

Only after the candidate and penalty are fixed do we use the 14 final test
speeches. The model scores `r round(live_accuracy, 4)` accuracy and
`r round(live_bal_accuracy, 4)` balanced accuracy. The majority label learned
from training would score `r round(split_baseline_accuracy, 4)` on this exact
test set. That rate is below 0.5 because the training majority is
`1900 or later`, while this test split contains more `before 1900` paragraphs.

Keeping speeches whole does not preserve the corpus class mix. The corpus-wide
largest-class baseline is `r round(corpus_baseline, 4)`, but the same-split
comparison is the one a deployable rule could use.

## What the fit did not prove

A fitted model contains a fixed recipe and learned weights. It gives labels to new rows
with the same structure as the training rows. It does not establish that the
label is appropriate or that the corpus represents other text. It also cannot
guarantee performance under a harder split. The next lesson examines
sensitivity to repeated splits.

## What to remember

- A pilot corpus can teach labeling without being large enough for a test of a model.
- A grouped test set with four rows cannot measure much.
- A speech-held-out split keeps one address from leaking across both sides.
- Grouped folds compare candidates without using the final test set.
- A recipe, model specification, engine, and workflow have different jobs.
- Tf-idf gives more weight to words that are common in one paragraph and rare in
  the rest.
- A model score needs a baseline beside it.

A trained classifier requires further evaluation. Its score must remain useful
under a more demanding test.
